It provides advanced secondary treatment of domestic, commercial, and industrial wastewater for the cities of Belmont, San Carlos, Redwood City, and Woodside; and for the service area of the West Bay Sanitary District, which collects wastewater from the cities of Menlo Park, Atherton, and Portola Valley, and areas of East Palo Alto, Woodside, and unincorporated San Mateo and Santa Clara counties. The Facility serves a population of about 220,000 people. Attachment B provides a map and aerial photo of the area around the treatment plant. 2.1.2 Collection System. The Discharger’s wastewater collection system is part of the Facility covered by this Order. It consists of approximately nine miles of force main and four pump stations, which receive wastewater from four satellite wastewater collection systems (West Bay Sanitary District, City of Belmont, City of San Carlos, and City of Redwood City). Wastewater travels by gravity to the four pump stations and then by force main to the treatment plant. During wet weather, the plant’s booster station and influent lift station may be used to handle elevated force main flows. chunks.text: Primary sedimentation is to remove the suspended solids (SS) by controlling the water flow velocity. It is required the settling time of SS shorter than the water travelling time in the tank. The SS with low density (1.1 g/mL and 1.5 g/mL) or small size but high density (1.5 g/mL) is the target pollutants to be removed in primary clarification. Most abundant MPs in the wastewater is PET followed by PE and PP (Fig. 2b ). The density of PET is between 0.96 and 1.45 g/mL. It is predicted that the primary sedimentation would catch the MPs consist of PET. However, PE and PP are difficult to be removed as they have density lower than water. Hence, wastewater containing large amount of moderate-density MPs would have high MPs removal during primary treatment.

chunks.text: The secondary clarifier is a 10-layer non-reactive system labelled from the bottom to the top. It has a total height of 4 m, and occupies a surface area of 1500 m 2 and a volume of 6000 m 3 . The tank is fed from the 6th, treated water is harvested from the 10th, and the settled sludge flows out from the first layer. A fraction of the sludge flows out of the system in the form of waste at a flow rate of 385 m 3 /d, corresponding to a biomass age of 9 days, while the other fraction is recycled externally to the first tank at a rate of 18,446 m 3 /d. The biological processes occurring in both biological reactors are simulated using the IWA Activated Sludge Model No. 1 (ASM1) proposed by [47] . This model uses thirteen state variables to track the fate of biodegradable, non-biodegradable, soluble, insoluble, nitrogen, and carbon materials. These state variables are linked to eight degradation bioprocesses occurring in biological reactors.

chunks.text: A pilot-scale system, consisting of a grit tank and microscreen for primary treatment followed by a SAF-MBR 2.0 for secondary treatment, was installed at the Codiga Resource Recovery Center (Stanford, CA), as illustrated in. The pilot-scale system treated municipal wastewater pumped from the Serra Street sewer on the Stanford campus for more than three years. Sewage was de-gritted in a grit tank then subject to primary treatment by screening through a 0.3 mm pore size microscreen (MS-28, Hydro International). The pilot-scale SAF-MBR 2.0 consisted of: (1) two AFBRs operated in parallel, hereafter referred to as AFBR 1 and AFBR 2, containing fluidized GAC biocarrier, and (2) a gas-sparged membrane tank equipped with ultrafiltration membranes. Recirculation of bulk fluid (twice the influent flow rate) between the three reactors enabled complete mixing and control of solids accumulation within the gas-sparged membrane tank.

chunks.text: Screens and grit removal are widely employed in WWTPs as they enhance the operation and maintenance of subsequent treatment units. Recent innovations in pretreatment technologies have brought the heavy cost of grit in WWTPs operations lower which has been considered an unavoidable burden. For example, based on advanced Grit Management™, Headcell® grit separation system was developed to achieve optimum grit removal for more than 30 years in the UK and USA. Headcell® is capable of achieving 95% removal of all grit 75 μm and larger. Because of its no-moving part design involving a hydraulically driven system, it delivers grit removal over a wide range of flows in a much smaller energy footprint than the conventional removal systems (Barter and Sherony, 2011) . Table 5 lists several such advanced technologies currently being considered for pilot, demonstration, and full-scale operations in the North America.

chunks.text: The coagulation process has been extensively employed because it is an effective, efficient, and easy way to treat water and wastewater. The selection procedure, as well as the coagulant dose applied to the wastewater, is critical. Thus, the number of researchers who have investigated hybrid materials (inorganic-inorganic, organic-natural, & inorganic-organic) has increased in recent years (Bobadilla et al., 2019) . Some factors that influence the efficacy of the coagulation process are coagulant type and dose (Abu Bakar and Halim, 2013; Huang et al., 2013) , effluent pH (Cao et al., 2011; Cao et al., 2010a) , mixing speed and interval (time) (Ernest et al., 2017; Tie et al., 2015; Xiao et al., 2009) , and temperature (Chaibakhsh et al., 2014; Ernest et al., 2017) . Optimising these parameters is critical to boost coagulation treatment efficiency.

chunks.text: Electrochemical treatment systems have been shown to provide effective treatment of latrine wastewater. Greater than 5-log inactivation of bacterial and viral indicator organisms is achieved via production of reactive chlorine species from chloride (15−20 mM) within 1 h at 4 V applied cell potential. 3 A combination of reactive chlorine species and direct oxidation provide reduction of chemical oxygen demand (COD) 4 and transformation of trace organic contaminants within 4 h (3.5− 4.5 V applied cell potential) 5−7 with rates enhanced at elevated chloride concentrations (up to 75 mM). Under similar operating conditions, ammonium removal occurs via breakpoint chlorination, 8 and phosphorus can be precipitated as hydroxyapatite. 9 Unfortunately, strongly oxidizing conditions in the presence of the high concentrations of chloride and organic matter typical of latrine wastewater also result in formation of toxic byproducts. 10 While wastewater disinfection is essential to protecting human health, an ideal electrochemical system should also be designed to minimize toxic byproduct formation. 11 Chloride enhances electrochemical treatment via formation of reactive chlorine species (e.g., hypochlorous acid, chloramines, and chlorine radicals).

chunks.text: To understand and address these issues, we perform a case study for water and energy recovery at different geographic scales in which design components are integrated for quantitative assessment of scale configurations. We define and analyze different configurations (Figure 1 ) and rank them using a multicriteria decision analysis (MCDA) tool 13 that is widely used for environment and energy research. 14, 15 2.2. Case Study. For our case study, we choose the service area of the City of Palo Alto Regional Water Quality Control Plant (PARWQCP), located in Santa Clara County, California, U.S.A. The City of Palo Alto owns and operates the PARWQCP, a centralized treatment plant that serves the communities of Mountain View, Palo Alto, Los Altos, Los Altos Hills, Stanford University, and East Palo Alto Sanitary District (Supporting Information Figure S1 ). For the purposes of this case study, we used data for FY 2007−2008 because a detailed audit of water is available for that time period. Most of the information remains relevant as of 2013. The PARWQCP treats ∼87 000 m 3 per day (∼23 MGD) of wastewater generated by 220 000 residents.

Specifically, plants A, B, and C experienced a reduction in CFP of 7.55%, 9.5%, and 10.59%, respectively. This is because greater particulate settling in the primary clarifier results in lower CO 2 emissions from microbial respiration and higher waste sludge  contents in the AD process (Gori et al., 2011 (Gori et al., , 2013)) . In terms of CO 2 emissions, the AD ranked third after PG, with 0.019, 0.039, and 0.34 kg CO 2 /kg COD rem. for plants A, B, and C, respectively. chunks.text: The secondary biological treatment consists of two carrousel-shaped biological reactors with suspended biomass, equipped with two horizontal aerators, which include nitrogen removal. Regarding the sludge line, a fraction of the solids settled in the secondary settler is purged to the sludge thickener. Previously to the band filter, the sludge passes through a homogenizer to be mixed with cationic polyelectrolyte and further dewatered in the band filter prior being stored in a silo. Calafell WWTP was built on 1994 to treat the wastewaters of the municipalities of Calafell and Bellveí and designed for 70,000 population equivalent with a maximum flow of 12,000 m 3 /day. After a primary treatment, wastewater is treated in two activated sludge reactors with extended aeration including nitrogen removal, followed by the secondary settler. From these units, the treated wastewater is directly discharged to the submarine sewage. Some differences are observed in the operation of the plant between winter and summer seasons due to fluctuations on the population and changes on the influent composition. A coagulation-flocculation treatment, only operated during summer, receives the wastewater after the screening step.
